item.title: Texas high school football: Five Houston-area games to watch in Week 10
item.description: Pearland running back Royce Swan has 20 rushing touchdowns this season, (Jason Fochtman/Houston Chronicle) The penultimate week of the Houston high school football regular season features two marquee matchups between undefeated teams, with Pearland visiting Shadow Creek and Angleton facing Randle in games that will decide district titles. Atascocita has a chance to clinch its 14th consecutive playoff berth against Crosby, while Fort Bend Marshall and Crawford battle for district supremacy and the No. 1 playoff seed. Fulshear and Cypress Springs also meet in a key district clash with serious playoff implications. Here are five Houston-area games to watch this week. Pearland (8-0, 6-0) at Shadow Creek (7-1, 6-0) When/where: 7 p.m. Friday, Freedom Field What to know: No. 12 state-ranked Pearland and No. 9 Shadow Creek have already clinched playoff berths and are already locked into their divisions for the Class 6A playoffs, but the winner here will claim at least a share of the District 19-6A title with a chance to clinch it outright in the final week of the regular season. Pearland has been dominant this year and is now just two wins from securing its second consecutive undefeated regular season under coach B.J. Gotte. The Oilers have won 19 consecutive regular-season games dating back to 2024. The last team to beat them? Shadow Creek. Pearland hasn't let a single opponent come within 20 points this year, and the Oilers have the No. 1 offense in the district at 456.3 yards per game. They are averaging 50.3 points per game, which is on pace to break the program record of 46.7 from 2015, according to Pigskin Prep . Pearland excels at running the ball and has done so to the tune of 303.1 yards per game. Junior Royce Swan has emerged as a star in the Oilers' backfield and is among the Houston area's leading rushers at 1,271 yards with 20 touchdowns. Shadow Creek has a potent offense as well and ranks third in the district at 408.2 yards per game. Passing has been the Sharks' biggest strength, and senior quarterback Tavis Coleman has put together a superb season to lead the way. Coleman, a McNeese State commit, is completing 67.9% of his passes for 1,997 yards and 27 touchdowns without an interception. Sophomore B.J. LaFell, the son of former NFL receiver Brandon LaFell, ranks third in the district in all-purpose yards with 1,015 and has been a difference-maker on both sides of the ball. LaFell has contributed in several facets of the game and has scored a touchdown via rush, reception, pass, interception return and kickoff return. He also handles punting duties for the Sharks. LaFell, who has three interceptions, has helped the Shadow Creek defense become the No. 1 unit in the district at 120.2 yards allowed per game with 14 total takeaways. Senior Caden Watson is one of the Houston-area leaders in sacks with 11. Shadow Creek leads this series 4-2 since 2020, but Pearland earned a 21-14 victory last season. Poorman's prediction: Shadow Creek 27, Pearla

Atascocita has a chance to clinch its 14th consecutive playoff berth against Crosby, while Fort Bend Marshall and Crawford battle for district supremacy and the No. 1 playoff seed. Fulshear and Cypress Springs also meet in a key district clash with serious playoff implications. Here are five Houston-area games to watch this week. Pearland (8-0, 6-0) at Shadow Creek (7-1, 6-0) When/where: 7 p.m. Friday, Freedom Field What to know: No. 12 state-ranked Pearland and No. 9 Shadow Creek have already clinched playoff berths and are already locked into their divisions for the Class 6A playoffs, but the winner here will claim at least a share of the District 19-6A title with a chance to clinch it outright in the final week of the regular season. Pearland excels at running the ball and has done so to the tune of 303.1 yards per game. Junior Royce Swan has emerged as a star in the Oilers' backfield and is among the Houston area's leading rushers at 1,271 yards with 20 touchdowns. Shadow Creek has a potent offense as well and ranks third in the district at 408.2 yards per game. Passing has been the Sharks' biggest strength, and senior quarterback Tavis Coleman has put together a superb season to lead the way. Coleman, a McNeese State commit, is completing 67.9% of his passes for 1,997 yards and 27 touchdowns without an interception. Sophomore B.J. LaFell, the son of former NFL receiver Brandon LaFell, ranks third in the district in all-purpose yards with 1,015 and has been a difference-maker on both sides of the ball. LaFell has contributed in several facets of the game and has scored a touchdown via rush, reception, pass, interception return and kickoff return. He also handles punting duties for the Sharks. LaFell, who has three interceptions, has helped the Shadow Creek defense become the No. 1 unit in the district at 120.2 yards allowed per game with 14 total takeaways. Senior Caden Watson is one of the Houston-area leaders in sacks with 11. Shadow Creek leads this series 4-2 since 2020, but Pearland earned a 21-14 victory last season. Poorman's prediction: Shadow Creek 27, Pearland 23 Atascocita (5-3, 3-2) at Crosby (4-4, 2-3) When/where: 7 p.m. Friday, Cougar Stadium What to know: Three of the four playoff spots from District 17-6A are already locked in with C.E. King, North Shore and Summer Creek claiming them. But three teams are still mathematically alive for the final berth, and this game could ultimately determine who gets in. The scenario for Atascocita is straightforward. The Eagles can clinch their 14th consecutive playoff appearance with a win over Crosby on the road. For Crosby, a win allows the Cougars to control their own destiny. If they beat Atascocita this week and Humble next week, they're in. Atascocita has the No. 2 defense in the district at 281.6 yards allowed per game under first-year head coach Kyle Coats. The Eagles have created 14 takeaways in eight games, including nine interceptions. Atascocita has two Division I recruits on its defensive line with senior Texas commit Jason Johnson and junior SMU commit David Dotson, who, along with senior Landon Glaze, have combined for 35 quarterback pressures. Senior Houston commit Ta'von Bolden leads the district with 13 pass breakups, and senior Oklahoma commit Trenton Blaylock isn't far behind with 10. Bolden also has five interceptions and 49 tackles, both team highs. Crosby, playing its first season in Class 6A after moving up with the UIL realignment, has been steady on both sides of the ball under first-year head coach Jabara Williams. The Cougars' offense ranks third in the district behind C.E. King and North Shore at 347.7 yards per game. The defense, meanwhile, ranks fourth at 299.1 yards allowed. Senior quarterback Lott Robinson leads the district in rushing at 613 yards with nine touchdowns. He is averaging 9.1 yards per carry and is also over 1,000 passing yards. Senior Adam Sloan has led the defensive efforts and ranks fourth in the district with 77 tackles, including 10 for loss with 6 ½ sacks and seven quarterback pressures. Crosby beat Channelview and Kingwood before falling 30-24 in overtime against No. 17 Summer Creek last week. Crosby leads this series 2-0, but the teams haven't played since 2006 and 2007. Poorman's prediction: Atascocita 30, Crosby 21 Angleton (8-0, 6-0) at Randle (8-0, 6-0) When/where: 7 p.m. Friday, Traylor Stadium What to know: No. 3 state-ranked Randle and No. 4 Angleton have seemingly been on a collision course all season, and now the matchup has finally arrived in Week 10. The winner of this game will clinch at least a share of the District 11-5A Division I title with a chance to claim it outright in the final week of the regular season. But perhaps more importantly, the winner here will almost certainly secure the No. 1 seed for the Class 5A Division I playoffs. Since moving up to the Division I level with the UIL realignment, it's been business as usual for Randle. The Lions are averaging 55.2 points per game for the season and 69.8 points per game in district play. Randle has the No. 1 offense in the district at 498 yards per game with its rushing attack accounting for 74.3% of that production. For the fourth consecutive season, running back Landen Williams-Callis has already piled up more than 2,000 all-purpose yards. The five-star Texas commit is 1,744 yards away from surpassing Kenneth Hall as the Houston area's all-time leading rusher and is averaging 269.6 rushing yards per game in district play. But it's not just about the offense at Randle. The Lions also have the No. 1 defense in the district at 104.7 yards allowed per game. The team boasts a plus-18 turnover ratio with 19 defensive takeaways (eight interceptions, 11 fumble recoveries) and have just one turnover on offense all season, which came on an interception during its season opener against South Oak Cliff. Angleton is coming off a 28-21 victory against Friendswood last week, scoring the go-ahead touchdown with just 59 seconds remaining. The Wildcats are second to Randle in the district on offense (471.2 yards per game) and defense (162 yards allowed per game) and are surrendering just 7.3 points per game with four shutouts. Senior running back Jayden Moore is averaging more than 100 rushing yards per game and 10.5 yards per carry with 12 touchdowns. Senior quarterback Trey Gardner is second in the district in passing yards with 1,111 and has 11 touchdowns against just four interceptions while completing 65.6% of his passes. Sophomore John David Brittain is helping to lead the defensive efforts with a team-high 64 tackles, including 11 for loss. Two-way standout and Duke commit Kasen Jammer has scored 13 total touchdowns and has 585 all-purpose yards. This will be the first meeting between the programs. Poorman's prediction: Randle 42, Angleton 30 Fort Bend Marshall (6-2, 4-0) at Crawford (7-1, 4-0) When/where: 1 p.m. Saturday, Hall Stadium What to know: The scenario at hand in this Halloween game is straightforward. The winner will clinch at least a share of the District 11-5A Division

item.title: 7 teams and 23 players from Central Texas to watch in the high school volleyball playoffs
item.description: Brooklyn Bradley makes a return for Round Rock. Round Rock won a non-district volleyball match at Vista Ridge 3-1 on September 1st, 2026. (Henry Huey/Special to American-Statesman) The Texas high school volleyball playoffs are here. UIL teams across the state can start postseason play Thursday, and all have the goal to reach their respective state tournaments . Who in Central Texas has a chance to excel? The American-Statesman takes a look at seven teams and 23 players covering all positions who could thrive this postseason. From 6A teams who shared a district title in Lake Travis, Round Rock and Westlake to a 5A powerhouse in Georgetown to one of the area's top outside hitters in Johnson's Mya Ibarra, here's who to keep an eye on as the postseason gets underway. (Teams and players listed in alphabetical order.) Central Texas teams to watch Anderson If they can get past a tough first-round matchup against Hendrickson, the Trojans (29-6) could stick around a while in Class 5A Division I. Anderson hasn't lost since Sept. 11 and went 13-1 in winning District 24. Outside hitters Piper Poage, middles Chloe Frizzell and Julyana Harris, and setter Henley Magee form the basis of a deep roster that will be a tough out. Georgetown Florida commit Amelia Albright is arguably the area's best player, but Georgetown has no weaknesses, which makes it a state title contender in Class 5A Division I. Outside hitter Mallory Milner, libero Jordan Pitkethley and middle Taylor Vett are just a few other reasons the Eagles (40-5), who only dropped two sets on the way to winning District 23, are primed for a deep postseason run. Lake Travis The Cavs (38-6) are peaking at the right time. They haven't lost since Sept. 29 and enter the playoffs fresh off a four-set win over rival Westlake. Featuring one of Central Texas' best outside hitters in San Diego State commit Gentry Barker, Lake Travis has as good a core group as anyone in Class 6A Division I Region IV with libero Xyanna Stephens, outside hitter Maggie Wheeler and middle Hannah Sawtelle. Liberty Hill The Panthers (42-5) didn't drop a set in rolling to the District 16-5A title and are one of the area's stronger threats to make the state semifinals. Realignment put them in Region II, meaning if they get that far, they'll have definitely earned it going against Dallas-area schools in Division I. Outside hitter Hannah Griffin is one of Central Texas' top players, but she's surrounded by a loaded roster that includes setter Ryann Mendoza, middle Macee Walters, outside hitter Bry Tuley and libero Summer Snyder. item.content:encoded: Brooklyn Bradley makes a return for Round Rock. Round Rock won a non-district volleyball match at Vista Ridge 3-1 on September 1st, 2026. (Henry Huey/Special to American-Statesman) The Texas high school volleyball playoffs are here. UIL teams across the state can start postseason play Thursday, and all have the goal to reach their respective state tournaments . Who in Central Texas has a chance to excel? The American-Statesman takes a look at seven teams and 23 players covering all positions who could thrive this postseason. From 6A teams who shared a district title in Lake Travis, Round Rock and Westlake to a 5A powerhouse in Georgetown to one of the area's top outside hitters in Johnson's Mya Ibarra, here's who to keep an eye on as the postseason gets underway. (Teams and players listed in alphabetical order.) Central Texas teams to watch Anderson If they can get past a tough first-round matchup against Hendrickson, the Trojans (29-6) could stick around a while in Class 5A Division I. Anderson hasn't lost since Sept. 11 and went 13-1 in winning District 24. Lake Travis The Cavs (38-6) are peaking at the right time. They haven't lost since Sept. 29 and enter the playoffs fresh off a four-set win over rival Westlake. Featuring one of Central Texas' best outside hitters in San Diego State commit Gentry Barker, Lake Travis has as good a core group as anyone in Class 6A Division I Region IV with libero Xyanna Stephens, outside hitter Maggie Wheeler and middle Hannah Sawtelle. Liberty Hill The Panthers (42-5) didn't drop a set in rolling to the District 16-5A title and are one of the area's stronger threats to make the state semifinals. Realignment put them in Region II, meaning if they get that far, they'll have definitely earned it going against Dallas-area schools in Division I. Outside hitter Hannah Griffin is one of Central Texas' top players, but she's surrounded by a loaded roster that includes setter Ryann Mendoza, middle Macee Walters, outside hitter Bry Tuley and libero Summer Snyder. Round Rock The Dragons (32-11) shared the District 25-6A title with Lake Travis and Westlake. With an attack led by middle Kerrington Thornton, outside hitter Brooklyn Bradley and setter Kylie Cavil, and an excellent libero in Isa Cordaway-Dreier, the potential is there for Round Rock to at least make the regional finals in Class 6A Division I. Westlake Perhaps what's scariest about the Chaps (36-9) is that they have so many talented underclassmen. Setter Kyrksen Cook and outside hitters Geralynn Byers-Veal and Clayton Kelly will return for at least one more season, but Westlake is loaded in the present, too. Libero Sunny McWilliams and middle Annabel McDuffee helped the Chaps to a share of the 25-6A title and are important pieces of a roster that should challenge to make the semifinals in Class 6A Division II. Weiss The Wolves are a dangerous matchup for anyone and benefit from being in Division II in Class 5A. Dynamic setter Ava Jackson has a talented pair of outside hitters in Deja Carroll and Scarlett Nachampassak to utilize, while middle Addison Gottschalk and libero Madison Ancira are part of a loaded rotation. Wimberley Reaching the Class 4A Division II final last fall, the Texans (41-4) appear to be ready for another long playoff run. Outside hitter Trinity Laney averages more than four kills a set, and with setter Bianca Mohr, libero Kara Thames and outside hitter Ellen Watson, few 4A teams can match Wimberley's talent. Players to watch (Note: Players cannot be from a team previously listed.) Piper Adair, McCallum: With an average of 4 kills per set, she's the Knights' top hitting option. Milan Benavides, Glenn: Talented defensive specialist is part of a talented Grizzlies team that could go a few rounds deep in Class 5A Division II. Nora Bettis, Austin High: Floor general for a Maroons team that finished second in District 26-6A, she averages 4.7 assists per set. Harper Bohnen, Cedar Park: The junior outside hitter leads the Timberwolves in kills, averaging 3 per set. Mia Davis, McCallum: Impressive senior setter helped the Knights go 31-14 in the regular season and finish second in District 24-5A. Sadie Jorgensen, Vandegrift: Averaging more than 10 assists per set, she helped the Vipers finish second in District 24-6A. Anna Kurz, Cedar Park: A key member of last year's state championship team, the senior libero averages 5.9 digs a set and brings playoff experience to the Timberwolves. Audrey Hedlund, Vandegrift: One of the area's more talented middles, she gives the Vipers a chance in any playoff match. Jazzlyn Hepburn, Bowie: Committed to Washington, the senior outside hitter averaged 4 kills and 3.8 digs per set in District 26-6A play. Jullia Howser, Stony Point: Energetic senior libero leads the Tigers in digs and passing. Mya Ibarra, Johnson: High-flying outside hitter, who averages 3.7 kills per set, is one of the area's better players and will be a challenge for any block. Ella Larbi, Stony Point: The Tigers won't be intimidated by anyone in the 6A Division II playoffs after being in District 25, and Larbi has the hitting talent to help them pull a couple of upsets. Jennah Lee, Glenn: Known for her basketball prowess, she's also dangerous on the volleyball court averaging 3.9 kills a set. Shelby Lippert, Hendrickson: Athletic junior middle does all the small things for the Hawks. Wesley McGinnis, Austin High: Averaging 3 kills per set, the senior paces the Maroons' attack. Isla Ornelas, Rouse: An electric setter who gives the Raiders a chance to play a few rounds in Class 6A Division I, she averages 8.3 assists per set. Avery Ralston, Rouse: A big reason the Raiders won District 24-6A, the senior outside hitter will be a challenge for any opponent's block and averages 4.2 kills a set. Lyla Rosas, Bowie: Senior libero averaged 5 digs per set in District 26-6A play. Parker Schurle, Ann Richards: Junior outside hitter reached double-digit kills six times in district play. Madison Sestak, Dripping Springs: Dangerous senior outside hitter leads the Tigers with 391 kills and 34 blocks. Jenna Tello, Johnson: An excellent libero, she's averaging nearly five digs per set. Eva Marie Thompson, Hendrickson: If the Hawks can get by Anderson in the first round, they can make a run behind the senior's hitting on the outside. Emily Varnel, Dripping Springs: The senior joins Sestak in giving the Tigers a dangerous hitting combination on the outside. She's come on strong in district play, hitting double-digit kills in three recent matches. Sign up for the Daily Briefing from the Austin American-Statesman. item.title: Kyle Larson’s Talladega Win Is Safe. NASCAR’s Yellow-Line Rule Isn’t
item.description: Kyle Larson, 2026 Las Vegas Spring, Cup. Image credit: Nascar9919/Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 4.0) Kyle Larson won Sunday’s YellaWood 500 by going from 11th to first on the last lap of overtime. Within two days, NASCAR was explaining a stripe of paint on its own podcast. The facts first. Larson’s No. 5 Chevrolet passed seven cars in the final quarter-mile at Talladega, beating teammate William Byron by 0.041 seconds. Ricky Stenhouse Jr. and Ross Chastain crossed the line right behind them. It was Larson’s first superspeedway win in 59 tries. He got there in the low lane, after Austin Hill dove low off Turn 2, shucked him into the middle lane and sent him from the lead to 11th. NASCAR reviewed final-lap SMT data and ruled that Larson stayed above the double yellow line. Post-race inspection came back clean, so the win stands. What the line actually punishes The double-yellow rule has existed at Daytona, Talladega and EchoPark since 2001. It was written to stop the apron from becoming a passing lane after a run of wrecks. NASCAR’s crew-chief handout at Talladega in 2020 put it plainly: go below the line to improve your position and you get black-flagged, and force someone else below it and you may get black-flagged too. NASCAR’s Mike Forde spelled out how literal that is in July, after Bubba Wallace was penalized on the last lap at EchoPark. Wallace went below the line beside Ryan Blaney and Carson Hocevar, said he tried to give the spot back, and ended up second anyway after a push from Ty Gibbs. Forde said on the series’ Hauler Talk podcast that giving a position back doesn’t matter, intent doesn’t matter, and finishing the pass doesn’t matter. A quarter-inch of improvement is enough. He called it a 27-point swing for a driver in the playoff picture. Pack racing at Talladega Superspeedway, where the double yellow line is the only thing separating the draft from the apron. Photo: Carol M. Highsmith / Library of Congress (public domain) A rule this strict needs better proof Put the two rulings side by side. At EchoPark, the standard was geometry, not intent: if a tire was under the line and a position improved, it’s a penalty. At Talladega, the same geometry cleared Larson. That’s consistent on paper. The problem is who can see it. A driver in the middle of a 40-car draft can’t see a painted line under his own left-side tires, and his spotter is watching traffic, not paint. The only people positioned to judge are officials with replay and data, after the fact. My take: a rule with consequences this big and evidence this fine-grained shouldn’t be a black box. NASCAR already walks fans through contested calls on Hauler Talk. The missing piece is showing the work, meaning the actual final-lap positioning data and camera angles, not just the verdict. If the line is going to decide races, the evidence for each call should be public. The loudest case for scrapping the rule hasn’t changed in six years. item.content:encoded: Kyle Larson, 2026 Las Vegas Spring, Cup. Image credit: Nascar9919/Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 4.0) Kyle Larson won Sunday’s YellaWood 500 by going from 11th to first on the last lap of overtime. Within two days, NASCAR was explaining a stripe of paint on its own podcast. The facts first. Larson’s No. 5 Chevrolet passed seven cars in the final quarter-mile at Talladega, beating teammate William Byron by 0.041 seconds. Ricky Stenhouse Jr. and Ross Chastain crossed the line right behind them. It was Larson’s first superspeedway win in 59 tries. He got there in the low lane, after Austin Hill dove low off Turn 2, shucked him into the middle lane and sent him from the lead to 11th. NASCAR reviewed final-lap SMT data and ruled that Larson stayed above the double yellow line. Post-race inspection came back clean, so the win stands. What the line actually punishes The double-yellow rule has existed at Daytona, Talladega and EchoPark since 2001. It was written to stop the apron from becoming a passing lane after a run of wrecks. NASCAR’s crew-chief handout at Talladega in 2020 put it plainly: go below the line to improve your position and you get black-flagged, and force someone else below it and you may get black-flagged too. NASCAR’s Mike Forde spelled out how literal that is in July, after Bubba Wallace was penalized on the last lap at EchoPark. Wallace went below the line beside Ryan Blaney and Carson Hocevar, said he tried to give the spot back, and ended up second anyway after a push from Ty Gibbs. Forde said on the series’ Hauler Talk podcast that giving a position back doesn’t matter, intent doesn’t matter, and finishing the pass doesn’t matter. A quarter-inch of improvement is enough. He called it a 27-point swing for a driver in the playoff picture. Pack racing at Talladega Superspeedway, where the double yellow line is the only thing separating the draft from the apron. Photo: Carol M. Highsmith / Library of Congress (public domain) A rule this strict needs better proof Put the two rulings side by side. At EchoPark, the standard was geometry, not intent: if a tire was under the line and a position improved, it’s a penalty. At Talladega, the same geometry cleared Larson. That’s consistent on paper. The problem is who can see it. A driver in the middle of a 40-car draft can’t see a painted line under his own left-side tires, and his spotter is watching traffic, not paint. The only people positioned to judge are officials with replay and data, after the fact. My take: a rule with consequences this big and evidence this fine-grained shouldn’t be a black box. NASCAR already walks fans through contested calls on Hauler Talk. The missing piece is showing the work, meaning the actual final-lap positioning data and camera angles, not just the verdict. If the line is going to decide races, the evidence for each call should be public. The loudest case for scrapping the rule hasn’t changed in six years. After a similar Talladega finish in 2020, Dale Earnhardt Jr. argued on NBC for abandoning it, and NASCAR’s Scott Miller answered that outside of a wall, nothing else would stop cars from running 12-wide down the backstretch. Ty Dillon, then a finisher in the top three, agreed the rule was worth keeping. That argument still has teeth. The new package makes the line matter more Here’s the part that hasn’t gotten enough attention. NASCAR cut the Talladega spoiler to 3.5 inches this fall, down from 4 inches at Daytona in August and 7 inches before that. It also lowered horsepower and moved the stage breaks, as we covered in our breakdown of the Talladega rules package . The goal was to let drivers build bigger runs and pass more. Bigger runs mean more cars charging low at the end, and the low lane is exactly where the yellow line lives. A package designed to create more last-lap moves will produce more last-lap rulings. NASCAR’s habit of managing by judgment showed up earlier in the same race, too. Forde said about 75 percent of the field was below minimum speed at one point while teams saved fuel in Stage 1. Rather than throw black flags, NASCAR messaged all of pit road, the field sped up, and no one was penalized. That’s a sensible call, and it’s the same discretion that fuels the yellow-line debate. We’ve seen NASCAR draw lines in odd places this season, including the painted-line penalty at Bristol. What it means for Martinsville Larson’s lead over Denny Hamlin is now 73 points with two races left, and the next stop is Martinsville Speedway on Sunday. NASCAR.com’s math has him clinching with 59 points on the day. He has finished sixth or better in seven of his last eight Martinsville starts and has one win there, in the spring of 2023. The gap is so large partly because Talladega’s two big wrecks hit nearly every other title contender, and because of how badly Phoenix cost him a 49-point lead a week earlier. Our Talladega points preview warned the race could swing 70-plus points. It swung 71 for Larson alone. If another yellow-line ruling decides a superspeedway race next year, the question won’t be whether the rule exists. It will be whether NASCAR can prove the call it made. Larson’s No. 5 Hendrick Motorsports Chevrolet on track at Pocono Raceway in 2022. Photo: Caleb Spicer / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0) Lead image: Kyle Larson at Las Vegas Motor Speedway, spring 2026. Image credit: Nascar9919 / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 4.0). The post Kyle Larson’s Talladega Win Is Safe. NASCAR’s Yellow-Line Rule Isn’t appeared first on Backfire Racing .

item.title: Paul Merson gives his reaction to poor Arsenal performance
item.description: Paul Merson gives his reaction to poor Arsenal performance Paul Merson insists Arsenal did not play well in their match against Fleetwood Town after they were beaten and dumped out of the League Cup last night. The Gunners have been one of the top teams in the country for decades, and they won the last Premier League title, so many people had written off Fleetwood even before a ball was kicked. Arsenal players also seem to have psychologically written off their opponents before the game, as their performances suggested that they were not prepared for a tough battle. It came back to haunt them as a hungrier and more determined Fleetwood beat them on penalties to reach the next round while sending Arsenal back home to focus on other competitions. Merson’s Criticism The Gunners have one less competition to worry about, but it was not their intention to get dumped out of the Carabao Cup by Town. Merson followed the game, and he was not happy with Arsenal’s performance as he insists the Gunners did not play well in the match. He said via the Daily Mail : “The work rate was there [from Arsenal], but the performance wasn’t. Gyokeres, Havertz, they can’t knock on Arteta’s door at the weekend. If one of them wasn’t playing, they couldn’t have any argument about it. They didn’t play well. “The one thing Fleetwood were going to do was work their socks off. Talent-wise, not even on the same planet let alone the same pitch, but you’ve got to match them. They matched them, but then you’ve got to do more and it was only Odegaard who did that extra bit.” (Photo by Carl Recine/Getty Images) A Wake-Up Call Merson’s comments show the importance of consistency to Arsenal’s success, and the club’s performance against Fleetwood was a major disappointment. Arsenal have to put this humiliation behind them now and concentrate on the upcoming match against Liverpool; however, this defeat will live with the club and fans for a long time to come. _____________________________________________________________________________________________ ADMIN COMMENT So here are some simple rules which I must insist commenters follow…. You agree not to give any personal abuse to other Arsenal fans. Everyone is allowed to hold their own opinions even if you disagree with them. It COSTS NOTHING TO BE POLITE TO OTHER ARSENAL FANS. item.content:encoded: Paul Merson gives his reaction to poor Arsenal performance Paul Merson insists Arsenal did not play well in their match against Fleetwood Town after they were beaten and dumped out of the League Cup last night. The Gunners have been one of the top teams in the country for decades, and they won the last Premier League title, so many people had written off Fleetwood even before a ball was kicked. Arsenal players also seem to have psychologically written off their opponents before the game, as their performances suggested that they were not prepared for a tough battle. It came back to haunt them as a hungrier and more determined Fleetwood beat them on penalties to reach the next round while sending Arsenal back home to focus on other competitions. Merson’s Criticism The Gunners have one less competition to worry about, but it was not their intention to get dumped out of the Carabao Cup by Town. Merson followed the game, and he was not happy with Arsenal’s performance as he insists the Gunners did not play well in the match. He said via the Daily Mail : “The work rate was there [from Arsenal], but the performance wasn’t. Gyokeres, Havertz, they can’t knock on Arteta’s door at the weekend. If one of them wasn’t playing, they couldn’t have any argument about it. They didn’t play well. “The one thing Fleetwood were going to do was work their socks off. item.title: Kamario Taylor is out vs Texas. But that shouldn't slow down Mississippi State's pace
item.description: Texas defensive lineman Alex January (right) sacks Mississippi State quarterback Blake Shapen (2) during the second half Oct. 25, 2025 in Starkville, Miss. (James Pugh/Associated Press) In last season's wild 45-38 overtime win at Mississippi State, Texas football found out what it's like facing the high-tempo attack orchestrated by third-year head coach and offensive play caller Jeff Lebby. The Bulldogs like to go fast. Like, really fast. And they like to use really fast guys. And that won't change even though Mississippi State will play the rest of the season without star quarterback Kamario Taylor. UP NEXT NO. 11 TEXAS VS. MISSISSIPPI STATE When/where: 6:30 p.m. Saturday at Royal-Memorial Stadium. TV/radio: ESPN; 1300 AM, 98.1 FM, 105.3 FM (Spanish). "Not only speed from play to play, but also the speed that they have on the perimeter, at the receivers, everything," said Texas defensive tackle Hero Kanu, one of eight starters on the Longhorns' defense who played in last year's game. "I know they use a lot of spread formations, open formations and vertical routes because they have guys that run like a 10.2 (seconds in the 100 meters)." But Mississippi State can get tough, too, said safety Jelani McDonald, who had a career-high 14 tackles last year against the Bulldogs. "Very, very tempo," he said. "But they're physical, too, you know? They just try to get you to either play to the run or play pass, so we've just got to be be able to come in, do our job, and get it done." MORE: Texas Longhorns look for an answer to their third-quarter struggles in SEC play Mississippi State offense among nation's best early in season But can Mississippi State unleash all that speed at the skill spots without Taylor? The 6-foot-4, 230-pound sophomore from tiny Macon, Miss., launched himself into the Heisman Trophy conversation after the first month of the season while helping the Bulldogs rocket into the national rankings. He threw for 1,450 yards and 17 touchdowns through the first five weeks before missing the Oct. 17 game against LSU with a right foot or ankle injury and then reaggravated the injury early in last week's setback against Oklahoma. Jeff Lebby (left) of the Mississippi State Bulldogs and Kamario Taylor (right) of the Mississippi State Bulldogs during the game against the Alabama Crimson Tide at Davis Wade Stadium on Oct. 3, 2026 in Starkville, Mis. (Justin Ford/Getty Images) In those complete games with Taylor behind center, Mississippi State averaged 48.8 points, including 54 total points while splitting a pair of contests against ranked SEC foes in Missouri and Alabama. Without him, Mississippi State had just 291 yards in a 31-0 loss at LSU and 352 yards in a 23-15 home loss to the Sooners. Lebby announced Tuesday that Taylor will miss the rest of the season after impending surgery to repair ligament damage in his right toe. Lebby said after the loss to Oklahoma that Puckett and Appalachian State transfer AJ Swann would both get practice reps wit

(James Pugh/Associated Press) In last season's wild 45-38 overtime win at Mississippi State, Texas football found out what it's like facing the high-tempo attack orchestrated by third-year head coach and offensive play caller Jeff Lebby. The Bulldogs like to go fast. Like, really fast. And they like to use really fast guys. And that won't change even though Mississippi State will play the rest of the season without star quarterback Kamario Taylor. UP NEXT NO. 11 TEXAS VS. MISSISSIPPI STATE When/where: 6:30 p.m. Saturday at Royal-Memorial Stadium. TV/radio: ESPN; 1300 AM, 98.1 FM, 105.3 FM (Spanish). "Not only speed from play to play, but also the speed that they have on the perimeter, at the receivers, everything," said Texas defensive tackle Hero Kanu, one of eight starters on the Longhorns' defense who played in last year's game. "I know they use a lot of spread formations, open formations and vertical routes because they have guys that run like a 10.2 (seconds in the 100 meters)." But Mississippi State can get tough, too, said safety Jelani McDonald, who had a career-high 14 tackles last year against the Bulldogs. "Very, very tempo," he said. "But they're physical, too, you know? They just try to get you to either play to the run or play pass, so we've just got to be be able to come in, do our job, and get it done." MORE: Texas Longhorns look for an answer to their third-quarter struggles in SEC play Mississippi State offense among nation's best early in season But can Mississippi State unleash all that speed at the skill spots without Taylor? The 6-foot-4, 230-pound sophomore from tiny Macon, Miss., launched himself into the Heisman Trophy conversation after the first month of the season while helping the Bulldogs rocket into the national rankings. He threw for 1,450 yards and 17 touchdowns through the first five weeks before missing the Oct. 17 game against LSU with a right foot or ankle injury and then reaggravated the injury early in last week's setback against Oklahoma. Jeff Lebby (left) of the Mississippi State Bulldogs and Kamario Taylor (right) of the Mississippi State Bulldogs during the game against the Alabama Crimson Tide at Davis Wade Stadium on Oct. 3, 2026 in Starkville, Mis. (Justin Ford/Getty Images) In those complete games with Taylor behind center, Mississippi State averaged 48.8 points, including 54 total points while splitting a pair of contests against ranked SEC foes in Missouri and Alabama. Without him, Mississippi State had just 291 yards in a 31-0 loss at LSU and 352 yards in a 23-15 home loss to the Sooners. Lebby announced Tuesday that Taylor will miss the rest of the season after impending surgery to repair ligament damage in his right toe. Lebby said after the loss to Oklahoma that Puckett and Appalachian State transfer AJ Swann would both get practice reps with the first team. Puckett, who started the LSU game, played the final three quarters against Oklahoma and completed 17 of 24 passes for 158 yards and one touchdown with 37 rushing yards. He threw one interception and lost one fumble. MORE: 'We're all human': Why Steve Sarkisian still isn't envisioning changes after onside gaffe Texas Longhorns defensive back Jelani McDonald (4) motions a thumbs down to Texas Longhorns defensive back Graceson Littleton (29) after defending a play during the game against San Jose State at Darrell K Royal–Texas Memorial Stadium in Austin, Saturday, Sept. 6, 2025. (Mikala Compton/Austin American-Statesman) Steve Sarkisian: Offense still up-tempo without Kamario Taylor Regardless of who starts at quarterback for Mississippi State, Texas coach Steve Sarkisian said his team better get prepped for a high tempo. Last season the Bulldogs piled up 445 total yards on a whopping 86 snaps in the loss to Texas. The since-graduated Blake Shapen threw for 381 of those yards on 26-of-42 passing while Taylor attempted just one pass and had one carry in a reserve role. "I think the first thing with Mississippi State (is) they play really fast," Sarkisian said. "I think they snap the ball with an average of 27 seconds still left on the shot clock. That's how fast they want to snap the ball. They spread you wide with their splits, and they play fast on the perimeter, and I felt like that hurt us last year in the game at their place." But Texas handled the tempo by Ole Miss just fine in last week's 31-24 win , and the Rebels are only one of two teams in the SEC that snap the ball quicker than Mississippi State. Ole Miss ranks sixth in the nation in seconds-per-play with 22.6 while the Bulldogs rank eighth at 23.0. Auburn has the fastest tempo in the league with an offensive snap every 21.7 seconds. What does all that speed and tempo mean for a Texas defense that leads the SEC in total yards allowed in conference play with 283.8 per game? "Get your cleats in the dirt and be ready to strike," defensive tackle Alex January said. Sign up for the Daily Briefing from the Austin American-Statesman. item.title: Georgia players, Outkast team up with Nike before first Georgia-Florida game in Atlanta
item.description: A limited-edition apparel and on-field collection from Nike, the University of Georgia and Outkast, in collaboration with Class Trip, celebrates the first Georgia-Florida game played in Atlanta. Photo: Nike The Georgia-Florida Game will be played in Atlanta for the first time in the rivalry’s history. As the players come from far and wide, some Georgia football players and staff will be wearing gear celebrating an iconic Atlanta duo. Nike and Class Trip rolled out a limited edition Georgia x Outkast collection ahead of the World’s Largest Outdoor Cocktail Party. [DOWNLOAD: Free WSB-TV News app for alerts as news breaks ] Brian Francis, founder of Class Trip, said the idea grew from a lunch with André 3000. “This started over lunch with André. He was telling stories about driving up to Athens to watch the Dawgs. Then we saw Georgia vs Florida was headed to Atlanta for the first time ever. Georgia’s football and its music, together in the city that made Outkast. They put Atlanta on the map. This is our thank you,” Francis said. Nike shot the Georgia x Outkast campaign in Athens over the summer with six NIL athletes from Georgia: cornerback Ellis Robinson IV, safety KJ Bolden, linebacker Chris Cole, tight ends Kaiden Prothro and Elyiss Williams and wide receiver Talyn Taylor. WHAT’S IN THE COLLECTION? The collection draws inspiration from Andre 3000 and Big Boi’s styles. Each item will feature a signature mark that combines the Georgia G and Outkast crown. The collection includes: a red wool varsity jacket with black leather sleeves football jerseys in cropped mesh and heavyweight cotton styles, rugby shirts a satin bomber heavyweight fleece hoodies Max90 heavyweight graphic T-shirts cord caps, snapback hats and bucket hats. Nike and Class Trip also created on field gear and premium sideline apparel for Georgia athletes, coaches and staff. Those items include eye shield decals, skullcaps, wristbands, mouthguards and three styles of gloves with Georgia and Outkast graphics. There will also be a pop-up store at Mercedes-Benz Stadium for fans to purchase merchandise. HOW TO WATCH GEORGIA VS FLORIDA No. 3 Georgia and No. 17 Florida kick off at 3:30 p.m. LIVE Saturday on Channel 2. Channel 2 Action News will have a coverage of Georgia-Florida Game throughout the week. Channel 2 sports director Zach Klein will host a SEC GameDay on 2 special presentation Friday night from 7 p.m. to 8 p.m. A new GameDay on 2 airs Saturday at 11 a.m. with insight into the rivalry from our GameDay insiders Aaron Murray, Brandon Boykin and Champ Bailey. SEC GameDay on 2 postgame show will bring you reaction from the Georgia players and head coach Kirby Smart following Saturday night’s primetime game. [SIGN UP: WSB-TV Daily Headlines Newsletter ]

item.title: Today in Motorsport History, October 28: Hamilton Clinched a Fifth Title in Mexico in 2018 as Verstappen Won
item.description: Lewis Hamilton at Silverstone in 2018, the season he clinched his fifth title in Mexico City. Photo: Jen_ross83 / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 2.0) On October 28, 2018, Lewis Hamilton finished fourth at the 2018 Mexican Grand Prix and became a five-time Formula 1 world champion with two races still to run. Max Verstappen won the race for Red Bull, Sebastian Vettel finished second for Ferrari, and the title was settled in a way nobody would have drawn up: by a driver who said afterwards he had a “horrible race.” That mix, a champion crowned on a day he did not win and a race winner who never got near the title, is why Mexico City 2018 is worth remembering. It was the point where a long Mercedes–Ferrari fight stopped being a fight, and where Hamilton moved level with Juan Manuel Fangio on five championships. The competitive context The 2018 season had started as a real contest. Vettel led the championship by eight points at the halfway mark, and Ferrari had the quicker car at several circuits. Then it came apart. Vettel crashed out of the lead at Hockenheim, tangled with Hamilton on the opening lap at Monza, and failed to beat Hamilton in Singapore and Japan, both of which Hamilton won. By the time the paddock reached Mexico, Hamilton led Vettel by 70 points with 100 still available. The arithmetic was simple. Hamilton needed seventh place or better if Vettel won. Anything lower, and the title fight would carry on to the United States or beyond. Mexico City was also a track where Mercedes had been vulnerable: at roughly 2,240 metres above sea level, the thin air robs downforce and strains cooling, and Red Bull had won there the year before with Verstappen. What happened on race day Daniel Ricciardo took pole position for Red Bull, with Verstappen alongside in second and Hamilton third. Ricciardo bogged down badly at the start and Verstappen went straight past into the lead. Hamilton had started well but could not keep Verstappen in sight for long, and he was the first of the front-runners to pit, stopping on lap 12 for supersofts after his ultrasofts wore badly. That was the pattern of Hamilton’s afternoon. His Mercedes struggled to get its tyres to work, he fell back, and Vettel passed him for second on lap 39. Räikkönen ran a quiet race to third in the second Ferrari, and Hamilton could not get back past him. Ricciardo, who had recovered to run second, retired late with a hydraulics failure, his eighth retirement of the year, which moved Vettel up to second place. Verstappen won by about 17 seconds. Valtteri Bottas set the fastest lap, but he finished fifth, one lap down. Max Verstappen at the 2018 US Grand Prix in Austin, one week before his Mexico City win. Photo: HoverVan / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0) Hamilton’s fourth place was worth 12 points and lifted his total to 358. Vettel, with 294, could no longer catch him, since only 50 points remained. item.content:encoded: Lewis Hamilton at Silverstone in 2018, the season he clinched his fifth title in Mexico City. Photo: Jen_ross83 / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 2.0) On October 28, 2018, Lewis Hamilton finished fourth at the 2018 Mexican Grand Prix and became a five-time Formula 1 world champion with two races still to run. Max Verstappen won the race for Red Bull, Sebastian Vettel finished second for Ferrari, and the title was settled in a way nobody would have drawn up: by a driver who said afterwards he had a “horrible race.” That mix, a champion crowned on a day he did not win and a race winner who never got near the title, is why Mexico City 2018 is worth remembering. It was the point where a long Mercedes–Ferrari fight stopped being a fight, and where Hamilton moved level with Juan Manuel Fangio on five championships. The competitive context The 2018 season had started as a real contest. Vettel led the championship by eight points at the halfway mark, and Ferrari had the quicker car at several circuits. Then it came apart. Vettel crashed out of the lead at Hockenheim, tangled with Hamilton on the opening lap at Monza, and failed to beat Hamilton in Singapore and Japan, both of which Hamilton won. By the time the paddock reached Mexico, Hamilton led Vettel by 70 points with 100 still available. The arithmetic was simple. Hamilton needed seventh place or better if Vettel won. Anything lower, and the title fight would carry on to the United States or beyond. Mexico City was also a track where Mercedes had been vulnerable: at roughly 2,240 metres above sea level, the thin air robs downforce and strains cooling, and Red Bull had won there the year before with Verstappen. What happened on race day Daniel Ricciardo took pole position for Red Bull, with Verstappen alongside in second and Hamilton third. Ricciardo bogged down badly at the start and Verstappen went straight past into the lead. Hamilton had started well but could not keep Verstappen in sight for long, and he was the first of the front-runners to pit, stopping on lap 12 for supersofts after his ultrasofts wore badly. That was the pattern of Hamilton’s afternoon. His Mercedes struggled to get its tyres to work, he fell back, and Vettel passed him for second on lap 39. Räikkönen ran a quiet race to third in the second Ferrari, and Hamilton could not get back past him. Ricciardo, who had recovered to run second, retired late with a hydraulics failure, his eighth retirement of the year, which moved Vettel up to second place. Verstappen won by about 17 seconds. Valtteri Bottas set the fastest lap, but he finished fifth, one lap down. Max Verstappen at the 2018 US Grand Prix in Austin, one week before his Mexico City win. Photo: HoverVan / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0) Hamilton’s fourth place was worth 12 points and lifted his total to 358. Vettel, with 294, could no longer catch him, since only 50 points remained. It was Hamilton’s fifth championship, following 2008, 2014, 2015 and 2017, and the second he had won in a row. Afterwards he called it “a very strange feeling,” which matched a title won on a day when he was never in contention for the victory. Why Mexico 2018 mattered For Hamilton, the result moved him past the clutch of four-time champions into territory occupied only by Fangio, with five, and Michael Schumacher, with seven. He finished the season on 408 points after 11 wins, 88 clear of Vettel, and Mercedes went on to take its fifth straight constructors’ championship in Brazil a fortnight later. Sebastian Vettel, Hamilton’s title rival in 2018, at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix. Photo: ibrahimferhadli / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0) For Verstappen, it was a fifth career win, his second in succession in Mexico City, and the first time he had won twice at the same venue. He had never started a race from pole, which made the milestone unusual, and it confirmed the speed Red Bull had shown since mid-season. It also lands differently in hindsight: Ricciardo, who retired from the lead battle that day and said he could not see the point of the final two races, left Red Bull for Renault at the end of the year, leaving Verstappen as the team’s clear number one. Ferrari took the opposite lesson. The team had a car good enough to fight for the title and let the lead slip through mistakes, with Vettel’s crash from the lead in Germany the clearest example. That reputation for squandering good seasons stuck to the team for years. The lasting effect Hamilton did not stop at five. He took a sixth title in 2019 and a seventh in 2020, equalling Schumacher’s record, and the milestone he reached in Mexico started the run that made that possible. We covered the next big step in his chase, his record-equalling win at the Nürburgring, in Hamilton Equals Schumacher’s 91 Wins at the 2020 Eifel Grand Prix . Mexico City has stayed a place where seasons turn. The track’s history includes Gerhard Berger’s first win for Benetton in 1986 , and this year’s race has its own title story, with Kimi Antonelli’s 123-point lead leaving 125 points to play for. If you like title deciders with an odd twist, see how Prost won the 1989 title at Suzuka after Senna won on the road, or Mansell’s tyre explosion in Adelaide handed the 1986 crown to Prost. For the other side of Hamilton’s era, there is also Horner’s account of the Lauda tip that took Hamilton to Mercedes . Featured image: Lewis Hamilton at Silverstone, 2018. Photo: Jen_ross83 / Wikimedia Commons, licensed under CC BY 2.0 . The post Today in Motorsport History, October 28: Hamilton Clinched a Fifth Title in Mexico in 2018 as Verstappen Won appeared first on Backfire Racing .

item.title: Real Madrid apologizes after Kylian Mbappe controversy: ‘Our club holds deep respect for China’
item.description: Real Madrid apologizes after Kylian Mbappe controversy: ‘Our club holds deep respect for China’ appeared first on ClutchPoints . Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here . France captain and Real Madrid forward Kylian Mbappe is currently going through a rough patch. Just hours after losing the 2026 Ballon d’Or to Harry Kane, Mbappe also lost several of his collaborations and sponsorships with Chinese companies worth a few million . The controversy began after a video went viral in which Mbappé was heard saying that the funniest meme he had seen of himself was one where his face had been photoshopped onto that of a dictator. And the person in question was Mao Zedong. In China, creating satire or jokes about Mao Zedong, who ruled from 1949 until he died in 1976, is considered disrespectful and remains a social taboo. Shortly after the controversy became a worldwide phenomenon and had everyone talking, Mbappe officially apologized , followed by apologies from the La Liga president. Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial) Chinese beverage brand Dongpeng and dairy companies Mengniu and Milkground ended their collaboration with Mbappe, and this was soon followed by CMG, which also banned the broadcast of La Liga in the nation. With both a vast reputation and considerable financial stakes involved, Real Madrid, Mbappe’s club, has now publicly apologised . “Real Madrid C. F. wishes to express its apologies to the Chinese people for any discomfort that may have been caused by the recent words of our player Kylian Mbappé. Our club holds deep respect for China, its history, its culture, and its citizens, as well as for the millions of Chinese fans who feel affection and admiration for Real Madrid. “The club joins the public apology expressed by Kylian Mbappé, in which the player himself has conveyed his regret for his words and reiterated his respect for the Chinese people. Real Madrid reaffirms its commitment to the values of respect, coexistence, and understanding among cultures, and expresses its desire to continue strengthening the bonds of friendship and affection that unite it with China and its citizens,” Real Madrid wrote. The French captain’s statement on Mao Zedong has been taken very seriously in China, with the Chinese social media app Xiaohongshu freezing Mbappe’s account, as well as Dior and Hublot removing their campaigns with Mbappe. Al Jazeera also noted that while Adidas stores in Beijing had Real Madrid kits on display, none bore Mbappe’s name. View this post on Instagram Related: Harry Kane spends wholesome moment with wife after Ballon d’Or win Related: Lamine Yamal breaks silence after losing Ballon d’Or; Father reportedly involved in violent airport incident

item.title: Henry defends himself after Ballon d'Or criticism
item.description: Thierry Henry finished runner-up to Pavel Nedved in the 2003 Ballon d'Or [EPA] Thierry Henry has defended himself after criticism over the way he hosted Monday's Ballon d'Or ceremony. The former France and Arsenal forward, who has come under fire for remarks he made towards Barcelona star Lamine Yamal, overall winner Harry Kane and co-host Kate Scott on the night, has addressed what he said was "people getting really excited about nothing". Henry, who was presenting the ceremony alongside CBS Sports colleague Scott, joked with Lamine Yamal about him winning a third successive young player of the year award. He also corrected Scott's pronunciation of Brazil legend Socrates' name and admitted he wanted fellow Frenchman Kylian Mbappe to beat Kane to the top prize. Addressing the Lamine Yamal situation, which received an audible reaction from the audience in attendance, Henry said he wasn't "checking his ego" and emphasised his admiration of the young Spaniard. On the night, he teased Lamine Yamal by saying of his young player award: "It's your third one, right? But is it the one you really wanted to win?" Speaking in a social media video on Wednesday, Henry said: "I'm a big fan of Lamine Yamal. I wasn't checking his ego at all - that you didn't like the joke, I can understand. "But don't do that, he's one of the players I'd pay to watch, I love him." The 49-year-old also responded to criticism over his response to co-host Scott's pronunciation of 'Socrates', claiming she was in on the joke herself. "You didn't like the joke, I understand, but please stop saying I disrespected Kate," Henry said. "I will never do that and you can ask her, she was on the joke with me. She did Soc on purpose, and I said Soc, so please stop inventing stories." Arsenal forward Bukayo Saka won the Socrates Award for his humanitarian and charity work. Henry added Kane was a "worthy winner" of the Ballon d'Or before telling everyone to "relax" after his support of Mbappe's claim to the prize. "I'm French and I was always going to back up and support my fellow countryman," he said. "I said to [Kane], 'You are a worthy winner, you deserve it, you are the example that work ethic is a talent, working hard is a talent'. Well done, Harry Kane - and I call him Sir Harry Kane since the World Cup. "So please, people out there, relax, relax. I love Harry Kane, I love Lamine Yamal and I didn't disrespect Kate. She was on the joke with me." Ballon d'Or in London - the most chaotic ever? Quillan has recorded four goals and two assists for six points in four games with the Abbotsford Canucks, which included a hat trick in Sunday’s game against the Calgary Wranglers. His addition to the AHL lineup has been a big reason the team has bounced back after a 0-2-1 start to being at the top of the division. Quillan also has 24 games of NHL experience, so if there was going to be a forward call-up, he would be the guy. Mandatory Credit: Sergei Belski-Imagn Images | Source: Lastwordonsports.com - Levi Pike, Editor As the Vancouver Canucks continue to navigate the reality that is a long 2026-27 campaign where wins will be scarce, one thing that they can explore is changing up what the NHL squad looks like. Quillan has recorded four goals and two assists for six points in four games with the Abbotsford Canucks, which included a hat trick in Sunday’s game against the Calgary Wranglers. Oct 25, 2026; Vancouver, British Columbia, CAN; Vancouver Canucks forward Brock Boeser (6) checks Minnesota Wild defenseman Quinn Hughes (43) in the third period at Rogers Arena. Mandatory Credit: Bob Frid-Imagn Images 2. Braeden Cootes – Centre Take this candidate with an asterisk attached, because a Braeden Cootes call-up to the NHL is not likely anytime soon, but if Cootes plays fewer than ten games this season, he will not burn a year on his entry-level contract, nor make himself eligible for a theoretical 2029 NHL expansion draft. General manager Ryan Johnson has stated that Cootes should get ample time in the AHL, and realistically, calling him up to play on a struggling team will not benefit him much in the long term. The only reason Cootes should get called up at any point this season is for when the games do not mean anything of worth in the standings near the end of the season. 3. Trey Fix-Wolansky – Right Wing Fix-Wolansky has had a great start in Abbotsford, as he leads the team in scoring with nine points in eight games. One disadvantage that may prevent him from getting a look at the NHL level is his size. At 5’7″ tall, he would be one of the smallest players in the NHL. However, given his decent work in the preseason and his 26 games of NHL experience, it may be worth giving him a stint in the NHL to see if there is a hidden gem of a player here. 4. Ty Mueller – Centre Mueller saw some NHL action at the end of the 2025-26 campaign with the Vancouver Canucks, where he scored his first career NHL goal. He has eight NHL games under his belt and was a big part of the 2025 Abbotsford team that won the Calder Cup. He could be a candidate for one of the Canucks AHL call-ups, as the NHL team could cycle through their farm team options throughout the season. 5. Kirill Kudryavtsev – Defence At the defence position, Kudryavtsev should be the top candidate to get called up. Given that Guillaume Brisebois has struggled at the NHL level and has been in the press box more often than not, at some point, Brisebois could be sent down to Abbotsford, while Kudryavtsev could get a stint in Vancouver. He is also waiver-exempt, which makes it easy for him to be called up or sent down without any fear of losing him to waivers. He has recorded two assists in five NHL games in his career. It would not hurt to give some of the AHL players a chance to show what they are capable of at the NHL level. It would also give management a better picture of the potential of some of the young players. If veteran players are being healthy-scratched once in a while, these AHL players could be the ones that will get a sniff of the NHL at some point, with Cootes being the potential exception, as his development is the one that management will keep a close eye on. item.title: 'We'll try to make them very happy' - Mikel Arteta demands Arsenal bounce back from Carabao Cup shocker and bring joy to fans at Anfield
item.description: Arsenal FC v Everton - Premier League 2026/27 - Getty Images Sport Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta has called on his players to absorb the pain of their shock Carabao Cup exit before turning their focus toward a massive Premier League showdown. The Gunners were stunned by League Two opposition on Wednesday night, leaving the Spaniard searching for answers ahead of a difficult trip to Merseyside. Gunners stunned before massive Anfield trip Arsenal's Carabao Cup ambitions came to a crashing halt on Wednesday evening as they were dumped out of the competition by Fleetwood Town . Despite Viktor Gyokeres finding the net to cancel out an early opener from the League Two minnows, the north London giants were unable to find a winner in regulation time and eventually fell to a 5-3 defeat in the subsequent penalty shootout. There is little time for the Gunners to dwell on the defeat, as a massive Premier League showdown with Liverpool looms on the horizon. Arteta is aware that his team must move past this setback quickly to maintain their momentum at the top of the table. "We need to take it now on the chin. We are out of the competition, we’re very sad for all the people as well here who came to watch the game - I wanted to give them the victory. Now we need to recover, and get ready for Anfield," said Arteta on the club's official website . Repaying the travelling faithful Nearly 1,000 Arsenal supporters made the long journey to support the team, and their vocal backing was not lost on the manager. Despite the poor result, the fans stayed to show their appreciation for the players, and Arteta is determined to repay that loyalty with a big performance in their next outing. This match marked the beginning of a challenging run of three consecutive away fixtures, making a positive response against Liverpool even more vital for the club's season objectives. Addressing the fans' commitment, Arteta issued a rallying cry ahead of the weekend. "They are always with us. That’s unquestionable, after the game they showed their appreciation to the team, and we’ll try to make them very happy against Liverpool," he stated. Arteta refuses to blame committed players The result from Highbury stadium marks one of the most disappointing nights of Arteta’s tenure, leaving the Premier League leaders to reflect on a missed opportunity for silverware. The Spanish manager was quick to acknowledge the achievement of the opposition while expressing his deep disappointment at the final outcome. Arteta refused to lay the blame at the feet of his squad's effort levels. "Obviously, a really sad day for us. There’s nothing to criticise the players for in terms of their attitude, their application, their determination to go and play the game that we had to play, but obviously we conceded that really poor goal to start with and gave them some belief," the manager explained. Defining fixtures loom before international break Currently locked in a direct tie with Manchester City at the summit

item.title: Liam Lawson Lost 6 Seconds at the US GP Because of Car Malfunction
item.description: Liam Lawson heard a buzzing noise in his ears when the Virtual Safety Car was deployed in the F1 US GP, as he scored more points. Racing Bulls’ Lawson has been in rocket form since the get-go of the 2026 F1 season, and in a Grand Prix when none of the Top 4 teams faced any difficulties, the Kiwi ended up ninth to add more to his kitty in a fabulous season so far. Even though it was lonely for him during the F1 US GP race – unlike his band performance on Thursday – it wasn’t super smooth at one point when a buzzing noise distracted him heavily. Post-race, he explained what the issue was as the beep continued to disturb him, even though he slowed an additional six seconds to the delta. A delta time under the VSC is simply the time difference between a driver’s actual driving time and a time set by the FIA, which is a mandatory minimum reference. It is around 30–40% slower than a normal race lap and is calculated and shared with the F1 teams. A driver can be slower, but not too slow, than the delta time or match it. Lawson Points at Another Software Issue (Photo by Rudy Carezzevoli/Getty Images) // Getty Images / Red Bull Content Pool // SI202610260012 // Usage for editorial use only // He pointed out another software issue with the 2026 F1 cars, which underwent slow-speed testing on Friday after the debacle in Malaysia. “The VSC, when the VSC came out, we went into a double yellow, and we get alarms that basically beep when you’re going too quickly,” said Lawson to the media after the F1 US GP weekend. “It’s really loud, and obviously that’s basically to warn us not to be illegal on the delta. It was just stuck on the whole time. So, I thought I was illegal, and I’m slowing right down, and then I looked down, and I was like six seconds positive. So, I’m good, but a thing’s beeping in my ear. “It was extremely distracting, but I think it might have been a bug that everybody had. [Yeah], another software issue,” summed up Lawson, who otherwise was pretty elated to get the two points and finish ahead of Alpine’s Pierre Gasly. Lawson Credits Racing Bulls for All-Round Show in US GP (Photo by Logan Riely/LAT Images) // Getty Images / Red Bull Content Pool // SI202610260383 // Usage for editorial use only // He further solidified his own position in the Top 10 of the drivers’ championship in ninth with 77 points, while also helping Racing Bulls to now be with 102 points in fifth, with a solid margin over Alpine (69). It is a crucial fight considering millions are at stake, which helps on the financial end with better pay from F1. “For us, it’s been a very, very strong race and a strong weekend,” continued Lawson. “Qualifying and race executed well. So very, very happy. And obviously going to the next few races, some interesting tracks, but I mean the car’s been working well, so it should hopefully work well there too. “Obviously, with upgrades this weekend, it’s nice to see them working well. So yeah, I think we’ve done a good job at executing this weeke

item.title: Sergio Garcia And European Legends Face Permanent Ryder Cup Ban
item.description: Jerod Ringwald-Imagn Images A wave of European stars has officially departed LIV Golf, sparking hopes they might return to lead the Ryder Cup team. Yet a rigid regulation from 2017 keeps them on the sidelines. This rule blocks legends like Sergio Garcia, Ian Poulter, Graeme McDowell, and possibly Lee Westwood from serving as captains or vice-captains. The ban remains in place even as tensions between the tours thaw. Ben Parsons reported in Today’s Golfer that the DP World Tour is not expected to change this rule soon to accommodate the returning greats. The barrier stems from a specific regulation added to the tour rulebook in January 2017, long before the LIV Golf disruption began. According to Today’s Golfer, the DP World Tour stated: “Players cannot be a European Ryder Cup captain or a vice-captain if they decline membership of the European Tour or fail to fulfil their minimum event obligation in any season.” Most veterans lured by the breakaway league relinquished their membership for at least one season after joining. A sports arbitration panel in 2023 upheld fines and bans levied against those who competed in conflicting events. Current captain Luke Donald cannot pick from this pool of returning players as he weighs his assistants for the upcoming match at Adare Manor. Leadership roles fall to Edoardo Molinari, Francesco Molinari, and Padraig Harrington so far. Although Poulter and McDowell recently stepped away from LIV 2.0, they were once considered potential skippers prior to joining the Saudi-backed league. The Rule That Won’t Budge The path to leadership for these veterans is blocked by a technicality regarding tour membership. While players like Garcia and Poulter have left the Saudi-backed circuit, the damage to their eligibility was done the moment they dropped their European Tour cards. The rule does not distinguish between a temporary leave of absence and a permanent departure. It simply requires active membership and fulfilled event obligations in every season. As noted by Today’s Golfer, the regulation was designed to protect the integrity of the tour’s event schedule, but it now functions as a one-way door for captaincy roles. The DP World Tour has not signaled any willingness to create special concessions. The pool of eligible captains remains limited to those who stayed loyal or never left. Jon Rahm and Sergio Garcia have court-approved separations from LIV Golf and are free to go. However, their past actions regarding tour membership still count. Graeme McDowell added his name to the list of those leaving on Monday with a succinct message on social media. The complexity of this situation increases because numerous players based their choices on the fines and bans they received. In 2023, a sports arbitration panel confirmed these penalties, solidifying the rupture between them and the European Tour. item.title: Odegaard urges Arsenal to move on after Fleetwood upset
item.description: Fleetwood fans invade the pitch as they celebrate their team's penalty shootout win over Arsenal in the fourth round of the English League Cup (Darren Staples) Arsenal captain Martin Odegaard has insisted "we can't feel sorry for ourselves" and must move on quickly following their stunning loss away to fourth-tier Fleetwood in the League Cup. The Premier League champions crashed out 5-3 on penalties in an incredible upset after the fourth-round tie finished 1-1 in normal time at Fleetwood's home ground of Highbury. Arsenal's Bruno Guimaraes had his penalty saved by Jay Lynch in the shoot-out before teenage defender Conor Haughey scored Fleetwood's winner. Aaron Loupalo-Bi's first-half goal had put Fleetwood ahead before Viktor Gyokeres equalised after the interval. Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta made nine changes to his starting side but after a ragged first-half display he sent Norway midfielder Odegaard on for the second period. The visitors, last season's losing finalists, managed an improved performance but still missed several chances before teenage rising star Max Dowman was sent off five minutes from the end of normal time. "It's very frustrating to go out," Odegaard said. "Obviously, the way we've played was not on the level. We need to do much, much better than we did. "Frustrating, but congratulations to Fleetwood and we look forward to the next game already and bounce back. "They did well so we have to give them credit, but I think (it) was about us not being on our level, we need to do better. I thought we improved during the game, but again, we need to step up even more -- so that's a shame." Arsenal now just have days to get the defeat out of their system ahead of what promises to be a tough match at Liverpool on Sunday, with the Gunners having drawn level on points with Premier League leaders Manchester City last weekend. "We can't feel sorry for ourselves. We need to move on -- we have a big game at the weekend, so bouncing back at the weekend is all we can do now," Odegaard added. jdg/nf
item.content:encoded: Fleetwood fans invade the pitch as they celebrate their team's penalty shootout win over Arsenal in the fourth round of the English League Cup (Darren Staples) Arsenal captain Martin Odegaard has insisted "we can't feel sorry for ourselves" and must move on quickly following their stunning loss away to fourth-tier Fleetwood in the League Cup. The Premier League champions crashed out 5-3 on penalties in an incredible upset after the fourth-round tie finished 1-1 in normal time at Fleetwood's home ground of Highbury. Arsenal's Bruno Guimaraes had his penalty saved by Jay Lynch in the shoot-out before teenage defender Conor Haughey scored Fleetwood's winner. Aaron Loupalo-Bi's first-half goal had put Fleetwood ahead before Viktor Gyokeres equalised after the interval. Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta made nine changes to his starting side but after a ragged first-half display he sent Norway midfielder Odegaard on for the second period. The visitors, last season's losing finalists, managed an improved performance but still missed several chances before teenage rising star Max Dowman was sent off five minutes from the end of normal time. "It's very frustrating to go out," Odegaard said. "Obviously, the way we've played was not on the level. We need to do much, much better than we did. "Frustrating, but congratulations to Fleetwood and we look forward to the next game already and bounce back. "They did well so we have to give them credit, but I think (it) was about us not being on our level, we need to do better. I thought we improved during the game, but again, we need to step up even more -- so that's a shame." Arsenal now just have days to get the defeat out of their system ahead of what promises to be a tough match at Liverpool on Sunday, with the Gunners having drawn level on points with Premier League leaders Manchester City last weekend. "We can't feel sorry for ourselves. We need to move on -- we have a big game at the weekend, so bouncing back at the weekend is all we can do now," Odegaard added. jdg/nf

item.title: Chelsea’s defeat to Tottenham highlights the importance of decision-making under pressure
item.description: Chelsea’s defeat to Tottenham highlights the importance of decision-making under pressure Chelsea’s 2-0 defeat to Tottenham Hotspur at Stamford Bridge on Saturday exposed more than just tactical weaknesses. A costly mistake from goalkeeper Mike Penders and a red card for Cole Palmer turned an already difficult afternoon into a frustrating result for Xabi Alonso’s side. The defeat ended Chelsea’s hopes of securing a third consecutive Premier League victory and raised questions about how the team responds when matches become increasingly demanding. Beyond individual errors, the encounter highlighted a familiar challenge in competitive football: maintaining concentration and making the right decisions under pressure. Chelsea’s costly decisions against Tottenham The London derby offered a clear example of how quickly individual decisions can influence a football match. Chelsea had struggled to establish control against Tottenham, but the contest remained goalless until the 77th minute. That changed when Penders, making his first Premier League start, attempted to punch away a corner but inadvertently sent the ball into his own net. The situation became even more difficult when Palmer received a second yellow card, leaving Chelsea with ten players. Tottenham subsequently added another goal through Mathys Tel, securing a 2-0 victory. For Alonso, the match demonstrated how mistakes in crucial moments can undermine a team’s efforts, regardless of the preparation that takes place beforehand. High-pressure situations trigger a range of psychological and physical responses in athletes. The brain must process information in real time, including opponents’ movements, tactical instructions and positioning. Under the effects of adrenaline, some players thrive while others may hesitate or make mistakes. Stress can affect the brain’s decision-making processes, particularly when athletes have little time to assess their options. The same principle of decision-making under pressure can be observed beyond the football pitch. In online poker , for example, players also have to process changing information and make decisions within limited time, although the setting and nature of the decisions are very different. This illustrates how concentration and emotional control can influence decision-making across different activities, without suggesting that their outcomes depend on the same factors. For younger players in particular, the demands of Premier League football can be considerable.
